Tintagel
tin-TAJ-ul
n. (the north Cornish headland whose castle and Celtic monastery became the centre of the Arthurian legend)
Cornish Din Tagell, the fort of the narrow neck, from din, a fort, and a word for a constriction or isthmus.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Tintagel is the headland on the north coast of Cornwall where a narrow neck of rock joins a promontory to the mainland. There was a substantial settlement there in the fifth and sixth centuries, trading in Mediterranean pottery, and a Celtic monastic site on the island; the castle whose ruins stand there now was built by Earl Richard of Cornwall in the twelve-thirties, long after the period to which the legend assigns it. The legend is the point. Geoffrey of Monmouth, writing about 1136, made Tintagel the place of Arthur's conception, and from Geoffrey the whole Arthurian cycle grew, carried on by the French romancers and gathered up by Malory. By the nineteenth century the headland had become a shrine of that literature, and in the twentieth it drew the neo-pagan and the occult trade that still works there. The dictionary records the archaeology, which is real and interesting, and declines the legend, which is fiction presented as history; and it marks the headland as a case of invented tradition hardening into devotion, which is the exact process Scripture forbids in worship.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a legend as a chronicle of a saint's life, hence an incredible story; tradition as the delivery of opinions from father to son; a fable as a feigned story; superstition as excessive exactness in religion; and vain as empty or worthless.

expand to see more

LEGEND, n. A chronicle or register of the lives of saints; hence, an idle or incredible story.

TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices or rites from father to son by oral communication.

FABLE, n. A feigned story or tale, intended to instruct or amuse; a fiction; a falsehood.

SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigour in religious opinions or practice; false religion; belief in omens.

VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance; fruitless; ineffectual.

Key Scripture

Mat 15:9 — "But in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men."

Deu 12:32 — "What thing soever I command you, observe to do it: thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it."

Col 2:23 — "Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh."

Jer 10:5 — "They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not: they must needs be borne, because they cannot go. Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good."

Modern Corruption

North Cornish headland with a real fifth-century settlement and a Celtic monastic site, made the birthplace of Arthur by Geoffrey of Monmouth about 1136 and a shrine of that invention ever since.

expand to see more

The corruption is unusually easy to date. There was a place here, and then in about 1136 a cleric writing a history he largely made up assigned a birth to it, and the assignment has been treated as a fact for eight centuries. The dictionary calls Geoffrey's work what it is, a fable, and notes that the castle shown to visitors was built a hundred years after he wrote and seven centuries after the man he wrote about. Our Lord's verdict on worship built out of such material is exact: “in vain they do worship me, teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9). The rule that would have prevented the whole development is older still and is a rule about addition, “thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32).

The second paragraph names what the headland has become, because the trade there now is not antiquarian. Tintagel draws a steady neo-pagan devotion, with its shops and its ceremonies, and the dictionary declines to treat that as harmless local colour; it is religion offered to nothing. Paul describes the whole class of such observance as having “a shew of wisdom in will worship” (Col 2:23), self-chosen religion that looks impressive and feeds nothing. Jeremiah's mockery of the idol is the right note to end on, and it is a comfort as much as a rebuke: the thing cannot move, cannot speak, and “Be not afraid of them; for they cannot do evil, neither also is it in them to do good” (Jer 10:5). A legend has no power either, and the men who keep it are not to be feared, only told the truth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek maten (G3155), in vain; Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479), will worship or self-chosen religion; Hebrew yatab (H3190), to do good.

expand to see more

Greek maten (G3155) — in vain, to no purpose; “in vain they do worship me”, Matthew 15:9.

Greek entalma (G1778) — an injunction, a commandment of men; “teaching for doctrines the commandments of men”, Matthew 15:9.

Greek ethelothreskeia (G1479) — self-willed worship, religion of one's own choosing; “a shew of wisdom in will worship”, Colossians 2:23.

Hebrew tomer (H8560) — a palm tree, an upright post; “They are upright as the palm tree, but speak not”, Jeremiah 10:5.

Hebrew yatab (H3190) — to be good, to do good; “neither also is it in them to do good”, Jeremiah 10:5.

Usage

"“teaching for doctrines the commandments of men” (Mat 15:9) — Geoffrey of Monmouth, about 1136."

"“thou shalt not add thereto, nor diminish from it” (Deu 12:32) — the rule the legend broke."

"“a shew of wisdom in will worship” (Col 2:23) — the neo-pagan trade on the headland."
